questions.q: You want to know what is listening on your Pi and which process owns each port. Which command is the right modern tool, and why not the alternative?
choices: netstat -tlnp, because ss has been deprecated in favour of it.
ss -tlnp, because netstat is deprecated and slower while ss is the maintained, more complete tool.
ifconfig -a, because it lists both interfaces and their listening ports.
iptables -L, because the firewall table is where listening ports are recorded.
questions.explain: ss is the iproute2 replacement for the deprecated netstat - it is faster and shows more complete socket information. ss -tlnp lists listening (-l) TCP (-t) sockets with numeric (-n) addresses and the owning process (-p). ifconfig and iptables are the deprecated tools and don't answer this question anyway.

questions.q: Why is ifconfig considered not just old-fashioned but actually misleading?
choices: It only works as root, so ordinary users see nothing.
It is deprecated and can fail to show all of an interface's addresses, giving an incomplete picture; ip addr is the accurate replacement.
It shows too much detail, including kernel internals users shouldn't see.
It has been removed from Linux entirely, so it never runs.
questions.explain: ifconfig (and route, netstat, arp) are deprecated, and ifconfig in particular doesn't reliably show all of an interface's addresses - so you can be debugging a half-truth. The iproute2 suite (ip addr, ip route, ip neigh) is the maintained, accurate replacement.

questions.q: You set the correct nameserver in /etc/resolv.conf, but a name on your Pi still resolves to the wrong address. What is the most likely real cause?
choices: resolv.conf has a syntax error that silently disables it.
The resolution order comes from /etc/nsswitch.conf - usually an /etc/hosts entry (checked first) or the systemd-resolved stub is winning before classic DNS ever runs.
The Pi's DNS cache is corrupt and must be rebuilt from resolv.conf.
ifconfig is overriding the nameserver setting.
questions.explain: getaddrinfo() consults the hosts: line in /etc/nsswitch.conf for the order of sources. files (/etc/hosts) is checked first and can override DNS; the resolve backend (systemd-resolved's stub at 127.0.0.53) sits before the dns backend, which is the only one that even reads resolv.conf. Chase the order, not the file.

questions.q: In SSH public-key authentication, how do you prove who you are, and where does your private key go?
choices: Your private key is sent to the server and compared against authorized_keys.
The server holds your public key in authorized_keys and challenges you to prove you hold the matching private key, which never leaves your machine.
Both sides exchange private keys during key exchange to build trust.
Your password is hashed with the host key and that hash is your identity.
questions.explain: Public-key auth keeps the private key on your machine; it is never transmitted. The server stores only your public key and issues a cryptographic challenge you can answer only with the matching private key. This is one of SSH's two independent proofs - the other being the host key, by which the server proves itself to you.

questions.q: On a headless Pi you load a default-drop nftables ruleset over SSH. What is the one rule you must include, and why?
choices: iif "lo" accept, because without loopback the kernel cannot run nftables at all.
tcp dport 22 accept, because a default-drop policy without an SSH-allow rule cuts your session and you cannot reconnect.
ip protocol icmp accept, because SSH rides on top of ping.
policy accept, because default-drop is never safe on a Pi.
questions.explain: A default-drop input policy discards anything not explicitly accepted. Over SSH that includes your own session's traffic on port 22, so without tcp dport 22 accept you lock yourself out of a headless Pi with no remote undo. Always keep the SSH rule (and ct state established,related accept so replies to your own outbound connections come back), and test with a keyboard and screen attached.
